los.text: Describe how heart sounds may be altered in cardiac disease states and how valvular disease causes murmurs
los.html:
Normal
  • S1 = mitral + tricuspid closure (start of systole)
  • S2 = aortic + pulmonary closure (A2 then P2; physiological splitting on inspiration ↑ venous return to right heart delays P2).
Altered sounds
  • Loud S1 (mitral stenosis, tachycardia), soft S1 (mitral regurgitation, long PR)
  • Soft/absent A2 (severe aortic stenosis)
  • Loud P2 (pulmonary hypertension)
  • Wide fixed splitting (ASD)
  • Reversed (paradoxical) splitting (LBBB, severe AS)
  • S3 (rapid filling into a dilated/volume-overloaded ventricle: HF, MR; normal in young/pregnancy)
  • S4 (atrial contraction into stiff ventricle: LVH, HOCM, AS; never with AF)
  • Opening snap (MS)
  • Ejection click (bicuspid aortic valve)
  • Mechanical valve clicks
  • Pericardial rub.
MurmursTurbulent flow (stenosis of a valve, regurgitation through incompetent valve, ↑ flow (anaemia, pregnancy, fever: "flow murmurs"), septal defects).
MurmurTimingSite / radiation
Aortic stenosisEjection systolic (crescendo–decrescendo)Right 2nd ICS → carotids
Mitral regurgitationPansystolicApex → axilla
Aortic regurgitationEarly diastolic (decrescendo)Left sternal edge, sitting forward in expiration
Mitral stenosisMid-diastolic rumble (+ opening snap)Apex, left lateral position, bell, expiration
VSDPansystolicLeft lower sternal edge
Tricuspid regurgitationPansystolicLLSE, louder on inspiration (right-sided: inspiration; left-sided: expiration)
  • Grading 1–6 (≥4 has a thrill). Innocent murmurs: soft, systolic, no symptoms, normal S2 → echo if any doubt.

los.text: Describe the diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of aortic valve disease
sessions: Clin 2: Diagnosis and management of aortic valve disease
los.html:
Aortic stenosis

CausesCalcific/degenerative (elderly, commonest), bicuspid valve (younger, 50s–60s), rheumatic.
Symptoms (triad)Exertional syncope, angina, breathlessness (heart failure) → once symptomatic, prognosis poor without intervention (~2–3 years).
SignsSlow-rising, low-volume pulse, narrow pulse pressure, heaving undisplaced apex (LVH), ejection systolic murmur → carotids, soft/absent S2 (severe), S4.
Ix
  • Echo (valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4 m/s = severe)
  • ECG (LVH, LBBB)
  • CXR (calcification)
  • CT calcium score/coronary angiography pre-op
  • Exercise testing in asymptomatic.
Management
  • Valve replacement if symptomatic severe AS (or asymptomatic with ↓ LVEF <50%, abnormal exercise test, very severe): SAVR (surgical) vs TAVI (transcatheter: older/higher risk, TAVI increasingly first choice >75).
  • Avoid vasodilators in severe AS
  • Balloon valvuloplasty as bridge.

Aortic regurgitation

CausesValve (bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis, degeneration) or aortic root dilatation (Marfan, hypertension, aortic dissection, syphilis, ankylosing spondylitis).
SignsCollapsing (water-hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure, displaced hyperdynamic apex, early diastolic murmur (LSE), Austin Flint (mid-diastolic), eponymous signs (Corrigan's, de Musset's, Quincke's).
Management
  • Acute (endocarditis, dissection) → urgent surgery.
  • Chronic: echo surveillance
  • Surgery if symptomatic or LV dilatation/dysfunction (LVEF ≤50%, LVESD >50 mm)
  • ACEi/ARB for BP/symptoms.

los.text: Describe the diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of mitral valve disease
sessions: Clin 3: Diagnosis and management of mitral valve disease
los.html:
Mitral stenosis

CauseAlmost always rheumatic heart disease (women; immigrants from endemic areas); rarely calcification.
Pathophysiology
  • ↓ valve area → ↑ LA pressure → LA dilatation → AF, thrombus/stroke
  • Pulmonary venous hypertension → oedema, pulmonary hypertension → RV failure.
Features
  • Breathlessness, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, palpitations
  • Malar flush, AF, tapping undisplaced apex, loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at apex
  • Signs of pulmonary hypertension.
IxEcho (valve area <1.5 cm² significant), ECG (P mitrale, AF), CXR (LA enlargement: splayed carina, double right heart border).
Management
  • Anticoagulation if AF (warfarin, not DOAC, in moderate–severe MS), rate control, diuretics
  • Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (if favourable valve), surgical repair/replacement.

Mitral regurgitation

Causes
  • Primary/degenerative (mitral valve prolapse, myxomatous; chordal rupture), endocarditis, rheumatic
  • Secondary/functional (LV dilatation: ischaemic/dilated cardiomyopathy)
  • Acute (papillary muscle rupture post-MI → acute pulmonary oedema/shock).
FeaturesBreathlessness, fatigue, AF; displaced, thrusting apex, soft S1, S3, pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla.
Management
  • Echo surveillance
  • Treat HF (diuretics, ACEi, β-blockers) and AF
  • Surgical repair (preferred) or replacement if symptomatic severe or LV dysfunction/dilatation
  • Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (MitraClip) if high surgical risk.
Valve prosthesesMechanical (durable; lifelong warfarin: INR 3.0 mitral, 2.5 aortic) vs bioprosthetic (no long-term anticoagulation; degenerate in ~10–15 years).

los.text: Explain the pathology, diagnosis and principles of treatment and management of infective endocarditis
los.html:
Pathology
  • Microbial infection of endocardium/valves
  • → vegetations (platelets, fibrin, microbes, inflammatory cells)
  • → valve destruction (perforation, regurgitation), abscess (aortic root → heart block), emboli (septic), immune complex phenomena.
Risk factors
  • Prosthetic valves
  • Previous IE
  • IV drug use (right-sided, tricuspid, S. aureus)
  • Structural heart disease (rheumatic, degenerative, congenital)
  • Intracardiac devices
  • Haemodialysis
  • Poor dental hygiene
  • Immunosuppression.
Organisms
  • S. aureus (commonest overall; acute, aggressive; IVDU, lines)
  • Viridans streptococci (S. mitis/sanguinis; subacute; dental)
  • Enterococci (GU procedures)
  • Coagulase-negative staph (prosthetic early)
  • Strep. gallolyticus (bovis) → colorectal cancer association
  • HACEK group and Coxiella/Bartonella (culture-negative).
Clinical
  • Fever + new murmur (until proven otherwise)
  • Malaise, weight loss
  • Vascular phenomena (Janeway lesions (painless palms/soles), splinter haemorrhages, conjunctival haemorrhages, emboli: stroke, splenic/renal infarcts, septic PE in right-sided IE)
  • Immunological phenomena (Osler's nodes (painful finger pulps), Roth spots (retina), glomerulonephritis (haematuria), positive RF)
  • Clubbing, splenomegaly.
Diagnosis
  • Modified Duke criteria.
  • Major: ≥2 positive blood cultures with typical organism (3 sets from separate sites before antibiotics), echo evidence (TTE then TOE: vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation) or PET-CT (prosthetic).
  • Minor: predisposition, fever ≥38, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, microbiological evidence not meeting major.
Treatment
  • Prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics (4–6 weeks): empirical native valve: amoxicillin + gentamicin (BSAC; or vancomycin + gentamicin if allergy/MRSA risk/prosthetic)
  • Tailored to organism (e.g. benzylpenicillin for sensitive strep; flucloxacillin for MSSA).
  • Endocarditis team (cardiology, microbiology, cardiac surgery).
  • Surgery for heart failure (severe regurgitation), uncontrolled infection (abscess, fungal, persistent bacteraemia), large vegetations with embolic risk.
PreventionDental hygiene; NICE: antibiotic prophylaxis not routinely recommended for dental procedures (unlike ESC/AHA for high-risk patients).

los.text: Explain the development of the embryonic heart and major blood vessels, the formation processes of these structures, and the distinctions between foetal and neonatal circulatory systems
los.html:
Heart development
  • Cardiogenic mesoderm (week 3) → paired endocardial tubes fuse → primitive heart tube (beats ~day 22).
  • Segments (caudal → cranial): sinus venosus → primitive atrium → primitive ventricle → bulbus cordis → truncus arteriosus.
  • Cardiac looping (rightward D-loop, day 23–28) positions chambers.
Septation (weeks 4–8)
  • Atria: septum primum grows down (ostium primum, then ostium secundum forms) + septum secundum to the right → foramen ovale (flap valve) allows right → left flow in fetus. Defects: ASD (secundum commonest; primum in Down syndrome/AVSD).
  • AV canal: endocardial cushions → AV valves; defects → AVSD (Down syndrome).
  • Ventricles: muscular septum + membranous part (from cushions); VSD (commonest congenital heart defect, membranous).
  • Outflow tract: neural crest cells form the spiral aorticopulmonary septum dividing truncus into aorta and pulmonary trunk. Defects: tetralogy of Fallot (anterior septal displacement → pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD, RVH), transposition of the great arteries (septum fails to spiral), persistent truncus arteriosus; associated with 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge).
Great vessels
  • From pharyngeal arch arteries: 3rd → common/internal carotid
  • 4th → aortic arch (left), right subclavian (right)
  • 6th → pulmonary arteries + ductus arteriosus (left).
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerves hook under 6th (left) / 4th (right) arch derivatives.
  • Coarctation near ductus.
Fetal circulation(3 shunts bypass lungs and liver)
  • Oxygenated blood from placenta via umbilical vein
  • → ductus venosus (bypasses liver)
  • → IVC
  • → RA
  • → foramen ovale
  • → LA
  • → LV
  • → aorta (to head/brain)
  • SVC blood → RA → RV → pulmonary trunk → ductus arteriosus → descending aorta → umbilical arteries (×2) → placenta.
  • High pulmonary vascular resistance
  • PGE2 keeps ductus open.
Changes at birth
  • First breath
  • → ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance
  • → ↑ pulmonary blood flow
  • → ↑ LA pressure
  • → foramen ovale closes (→ fossa ovalis)
  • Clamping cord ↑ SVR
  • ↑ PaO₂ + ↓ prostaglandins → ductus arteriosus closes (→ ligamentum arteriosum) within days
  • Ductus venosus → ligamentum venosum
  • Umbilical vein → ligamentum teres
  • Umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments.
  • PDA: indomethacin/ibuprofen to close
  • Alprostadil (PGE1) to keep open in duct-dependent lesions.

los.text: Describe the signs, symptoms and pathophysiology / pathogenesis of acquired valvular diseases
los.html:
Rheumatic heart disease
  • Group A streptococcal pharyngitis
  • → molecular mimicry (M protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac myosin/valve tissue)
  • → acute rheumatic fever (type II hypersensitivity) 2–4 weeks later: pancarditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham's chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules (Jones criteria).
  • Acute: Aschoff bodies, verrucous vegetations along closure lines.
  • Chronic: repeated inflammation → fibrosis, commissural fusion, leaflet thickening, chordal shortening → "fish-mouth" mitral stenosis (mitral > aortic).
  • Prevent with penicillin.
Calcific aortic stenosis
  • Age-related "wear and tear" with atherosclerosis-like process (lipid, inflammation, osteoblast-like transformation) → nodular calcification on aortic side of cusps (no commissural fusion).
  • Bicuspid valve accelerates (presents ~10–20 years earlier).
  • → LV pressure overload
  • → concentric LVH
  • → angina (↑ demand, ↓ coronary flow reserve), syncope (fixed CO), HF.
Myxomatous mitral valve (prolapse)
  • ↑ proteoglycans, disrupted collagen (Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, idiopathic) → floppy, ballooning leaflets, elongated chordae → mid-systolic click + late systolic murmur
  • MR, chordal rupture.
Infective endocarditisVegetations destroy leaflets → acute regurgitation.
Functional regurgitationAnnular/LV dilatation (ischaemic or dilated cardiomyopathy) → poor coaptation (secondary MR, TR).
OtherCarcinoid (right-sided: TR, PS), SLE (Libman–Sacks), drugs (ergot, fenfluramine), radiation.
Consequences
  • Stenosis = pressure overload (concentric hypertrophy)
  • Regurgitation = volume overload (eccentric hypertrophy, dilatation) → heart failure, AF (LA dilatation), pulmonary hypertension, emboli, sudden death (severe AS).
